newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish militants in Hebron talk of war.
newsitem.headline: Jewish militants in Hebron talk of war.

text.p: Jewish militants talk of apocalypse.
Like the Jew who killed Yitzhak Rabin a year ago, they are up in arms over their government's plan to hand back land to Palestinians in a peace deal.
"There's going to be a war," Baruch Merzel, a leader of the outlawed anti-Arab Kach movement, told Reuters when asked what to expect when Israel pulls troops out of parts of Hebron.
Israeli-occupied Hebron is the home of a Jewish hardcore who view the West Bank lands captured in the 1967 Middle East war as their biblical birthright.
It is the only West Bank Arab town with Jewish settlers resident -- 400 of them live and study among 100,000 Arabs.
Once agreement is reached with the PLO, Israel will hand over parts of it to Palestinian rule.
Moshe Lissak, a Hebrew University professor of sociology, said an end-of-days scenario was key to the militants.
"These are people who are convinced that, from a messianic viewpoint...the Palestinians are foreigners here and must leave. There is no room for any political dialogue, no compromises.
"They think that war is inevitable. Not only is it inevitable, it is important because that will be the opportunity to solve the Palestinian problem by throwing them out," he said.
Ehud Sprinzak, a Hebrew University expert on Jewish extremism, said there were as many as 70 Jews in the hardcore surrounded by a few hundred followers. Several thousand sympathise with them.

They can come from Israel -- like Yigal Amir, the 26-year-old law student who killed prime minister Rabin -- or from the territories, though Sprinzak said a large number live in Hebron and the adjacent Kiryat Arba settlement.
Unlike the mainstream settlement movement representing some 130,000 Israelis in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, the extremists advocate violence, even against Jews, to defend their aims.

"I do not expect any political assassination in the coming year," Sprinzak said. "The possibility of an Israeli-Palestinian confrontation especially in the area of Hebron is, however, in my judgment, very high."
It has happened before. In Kiryat Arba, the tomb of a mass murderer takes pride of place.
"The holy Dr Baruch Kaplan Goldstein...(of) pure hands and pure heart, killed sanctifying the Name (of God)," reads the inscription on a grave in a large plaza dominating the settlement's park.

In February 1994 Goldstein gunned down 29 Moslems praying in Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, a site known to Jews as the Tomb of the Patriarchs and revered by both faiths as Abraham's burial place. He was beaten to death by survivors.
Like Amir, Goldstein acted alone. He had steeped himself in a militant religious fringe that Rabin had vowed to uproot -- before he was shot down at a Tel Aviv peace rally.
Lissak said another political assassination was possible.
"There are potentially people among them who could come to the decision to also attack the current leadership," he said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who opposes trading occupied land for peace, won Israel's May elections. But he has said he would honour deals, like Hebron, signed by the previous government. Militants label the deal betrayal.
"Anyone branded a traitor, it is in fact permissible and legitimate to destroy him, to kill him, that is the precedent (of the Rabin assassination)," Lissak said.
Ironically, before Rabin's assassination, Netanyahu led rallies where supporters chanted: "Rabin's a traitor".

After the Hebron massacre and after Rabin's assassination on November 4, 1995, in Tel Aviv, Israel briefly clamped down on Jewish militants, jailing a handful like Merzel without trial under emergency regulations. Kach was outlawed in 1994.
A commission of inquiry into Rabin's killing found fault with security forces for not acting on intelligence and anticipating a Jewish assassin.
Netanyahu's spokesman David Bar-Illan said plans existed for handling Jewish militants but they could not be talked about. An Israeli security source said he knew of no such plans.
One Palestinian told Israel Radio of arms being stockpiled in Hebron to fight the militants. The PLO denied it.

"I don't think that the government has done enough," Sprinzak said. He urged Israel to get mainstream settler rabbis, appalled at Rabin's assassination, "to open their mouths, start talking against extremism".
He said it was in the largely faceless middle circle where the next Goldstein or Amir may be lurking. Merzel agreed.
"Who knows how many Goldsteins there are around?" Merzel said, sitting in his dining room opposite a framed portrait of Goldstein captioned: "The saint Dr Baruch Goldstein".
Lissak said it might take only one: "We are sitting on a barrel of explosives, any match here could ignite a war."
